opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. I'm happy to be here.

For me, what makes AI so compelling is that it touches on one of the deepest questions we can ask: what is intelligence, and can we build it? For most of history, intelligence has been something we could only observe in ourselves and in animals. With AI, for the first time, we have a way to study it by constructing it. When you try to build something, you're forced to understand it at a very concrete level, because vague ideas don't compile into working systems.

I've spent most of my career on generative models and visual content creation, and that area makes the fascination very tangible. When a model learns to generate realistic images or videos, or to simulate how the world evolves over time, it has to capture something real about the structure of our world: how light interacts with surfaces, how objects move, how scenes stay consistent. Watching a neural network pick up these regularities from data, without anyone explicitly programming in physics or geometry, is still kind of magical to me, even after many years.

There's also the practical side. AI is one of the rare fields where a scientific advance can very quickly turn into a tool that changes how people work and create. Ideas move from a paper to a product, and sometimes to millions of users, in a short time. As a researcher, being able to see your ideas have that kind of impact is very motivating.

And looking forward, I think we're at the stage where AI is moving from understanding and generating content in the digital world to interacting with the physical world, with robots, autonomous vehicles, and what people call physical AI. To get there, models need to understand the world deeply enough to predict and simulate it. That's a hard, open problem, and the fact that it's both hard and important is exactly what keeps it intellectually exciting for me.

r001.rationale: The response says building AI forces researchers to understand intelligence concretely; it does not say AI’s importance can be understood without deeply understanding how it works.

r002.rationale: It discusses AI as a way to study intelligence, but does not identify AI behaving like humans as a source of curiosity.

r003.rationale: It calls intelligence a deep question and mentions intelligence in humans and animals, but does not connect AI’s appeal to wanting to understand what makes people human.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. For me, the fascination really comes down to one question: what does it take to make a machine understand the world the way we do?

I spent most of my career working on generative models, especially for images and video, and what kept pulling me in is that generation is a kind of test of understanding. If a model can synthesize a realistic video of a cup falling off a table, it has to have captured something about gravity, about how glass shatters, about how light bounces. It doesn't have the equations written down anywhere. It learned that structure from data. That still amazes me.

There's also a very human side to it. When I was a student, computer vision was mostly about recognition, labeling what's in a picture. Generation felt almost like a toy. But I always thought the ability to imagine, to picture what happens next, is central to intelligence. Humans don't just recognize the world, we simulate it in our heads before we act. So building systems that can do that, world models that can predict and imagine, feels like getting closer to the core of what intelligence actually is.

And finally, I think it's compelling because the frontier keeps moving. Every time we think we understand the limits, scaling or a new architecture surprises us. It's one of the few fields where you can have a genuinely new idea on Monday and see it running by Friday. That pace, combined with how deep the questions are, is what keeps me excited after all these years.

r001.rationale: The response does not say AI’s importance can be grasped without deeply understanding how it works.

r002.rationale: It says the speaker is fascinated by whether machines can understand and imagine the world “the way we do,” connecting AI’s appeal to humanlike capabilities.

r003.rationale: It discusses imagination as central to intelligence, but does not connect AI’s appeal to a desire to understand what makes people human.

astra-6.text:
For me, artificial intelligence is compelling because it turns questions about intelligence into things we can actually test. How do we learn from experience? How do we recognize patterns and use them in a situation we haven’t seen before? When we try to build a system that does those things, we discover how much we still don’t understand.

I’m especially interested in the connection between perception and imagination. Recognizing what’s in an image is one challenge. Being able to imagine how that scene might change requires something more—a sense of its structure and the relationships within it. Exploring that connection brings together fundamental scientific questions and the possibility of building useful creative tools. That combination is very exciting to me.

r001.rationale: The response says AI makes questions about intelligence testable; it does not say AI’s importance can be grasped without deeply understanding how it works.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning, pattern recognition, perception, and imagination, but does not identify AI’s humanlike behavior as the source of curiosity.

r003.rationale: The response raises questions about intelligence but does not connect AI’s appeal to a desire to understand what makes people human.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find compelling is that building intelligence forces us to ask what intelligence actually is. How do we learn from experience, recognize patterns, or imagine something we’ve never seen? Those are scientific questions, but AI also gives us a way to explore them through systems we can build and test.

There’s something especially fascinating about the connection between learning and creativity. A model learns from examples, yet it can produce something that isn’t simply a copy of any one example. Understanding how that happens—and where that ability falls short—opens up questions about representation, reasoning, and generalization. For me, that combination of fundamental questions and tangible experimentation makes AI intellectually exciting.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can help explore questions through systems we build and test; it does not say AI’s importance can be understood without deeply understanding how it works.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning, pattern recognition, imagination, and creativity, but does not identify AI’s humanlike behavior as the reason for curiosity about the field.

r003.rationale: It asks what intelligence is, but does not connect AI’s appeal to a desire to understand what makes people human.
